questions.q: What is the primary difference between a Dead Load and a Live Load in building design?
o: Dead Loads are determined by the building code; Live Loads are determined by the architect's preference.
Dead Loads are static vertical forces; Live Loads are dynamic lateral forces like wind and seismic events.
Dead Loads are gravitational forces from permanent components; Live Loads are transient forces excluding environmental loads.
Dead Loads refer to the structural frame only; Live Loads refer to architectural finishes and occupants.
questions.n: Dead loads are the constant weight of the structure and fixed utilities, while live loads are the non-permanent weights of occupants and movable items.

questions.q: In high-rise design, which type of load usually dictates the size of the columns and the lateral bracing system?
o: Axial Compression from cumulative Live Loads
Superimposed Dead Loads
Heavy Impact Loads from mechanical floors
Lateral Loads (Wind and Seismic/Earthquake)
questions.n: Tall buildings act like giant levers; the horizontal pressure of wind and ground movement governs the stiffness of the structural core.

questions.q: What defines an 'Impact Load' compared to a standard Live Load?
o: A load that remains constant for the duration of the building's lifespan.
A load that is distributed evenly across a large floor area.
The force exerted by wind hitting a curtain wall.
A load that is applied suddenly, requiring a higher safety factor due to dynamic energy.
questions.n: Impact loads (like elevators or moving machinery) create greater stress than their static weight alone suggests.

questions.q: How does 'Hydrostatic Pressure' affect a basement wall?
o: It exerts lateral pressure that increases linearly with depth, pushing against the wall.
It pulls the foundation downward through suction.
It reduces the wall's bearing capacity by making the concrete moist.
It only creates vertical uplift (buoyancy) and does not affect the wall's side.
questions.n: Water pressure acts like a triangle—zero at the top and maximum at the base—putting massive stress on retaining structures.

questions.q: What is the primary characteristic of a 'Thermal Load'?
o: The load caused by the installation of heavy HVAC ducting.
The weight of snow or ice accumulated on a roof.
The decrease in material strength as it reaches its melting point during a fire.
Internal stress created when materials expand or contract due to temperature changes.
questions.n: If a material is restrained from expanding or contracting as it heats or cools, internal stress builds up.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the behavior of Tension and Compression?
o: Tension causes buckling; Compression causes snapping.
Tension elongates the member along its longitudinal axis; Compression shortens it.
Compression is a lateral force; Tension is a vertical force.
Tension is only found in steel; Compression is only found in concrete.
questions.n: Tension pulls atoms apart, while compression forces them together, altering the length of the member.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of 'Shear Stress'?
o: Stress that acts parallel to the cross-section, causing sliding between planes.
The stress that occurs at the 'neutral axis' of a beam.
Stress that acts perpendicular to the surface, causing elongation.
The stress caused by uniform atmospheric pressure.
questions.n: Shear acts across the material, trying to 'slide' one part of the member over the other.

questions.q: How does 'Bending Moment' relate to the internal stresses of a beam?
o: It creates a combination of tension on one side of the neutral axis and compression on the other.
It is the point where the beam experiences the most shear.
It is the stress that prevents the beam from expanding.
It is the literal 'moment' in time when the beam begins to fail.
questions.n: Bending is not a single force; it is the internal couple of tension and compression that resists rotation.

questions.q: What does a high 'Modulus of Elasticity' (E) signify about a building material?
o: The material is very brittle and will shatter without warning.
The material is highly ductile and will stretch a lot before breaking.
The material is very stiff and will deform very little under a given stress.
The material has a very high weight-to-strength ratio.
questions.n: The Modulus of Elasticity is the ratio of stress to strain; the higher the 'E', the less it strains (deforms).

questions.q: What is the technical definition of 'Deflection'?
o: The twisting of a member along its long axis.
The vertical or horizontal displacement of a member from its original position due to load.
The cracking that occurs when concrete reaches its tension limit.
The permanent deformation of a beam after the load is removed.
questions.n: Deflection is the distance a beam 'sags' or a column 'sways' when forces are applied.

questions.q: Why is the triangle the fundamental shape for a stable truss?
o: It is the easiest shape to weld in a factory.
It minimizes the amount of tension in the bottom chord.
It is the only polygon whose shape is fixed as long as the side lengths are constant.
It allows for the maximum amount of interior roof space.
questions.n: A rectangle can become a parallelogram without side-length change, but a triangle's angles are locked by its sides.

questions.q: In a simply supported Pratt Truss under gravity loads, which chord is in compression?
o: The Vertical Web Members only
The Diagonal Web Members only
The Bottom Chord
The Top Chord
questions.n: Just like a beam, the 'top' of a simply supported truss is squeezed (compression) while the 'bottom' is stretched.

questions.q: What is the primary role of 'Web Members' in a truss system?
o: They provide a surface for attaching the roof purlins.
They resist shear forces and keep the top and bottom chords at a fixed distance.
They carry the primary tension of the entire roof.
They are decorative elements to make the truss look 'industrial'.
questions.n: Webs act like the 'web' of an I-beam, transferring forces between the two chords to ensure they work as a single unit.

questions.q: Why is a truss considered more 'efficient' than a solid beam for long spans?
o: Because it uses more material to ensure safety.
It places high-strength material only where tension and compression occur, eliminating 'dead' weight.
Because triangles are naturally stronger than steel.
Because it is easier to transport in small pieces.
questions.n: By removing the solid 'web' where stress is low, the truss achieves high depth and strength with minimal weight.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'Space Frame' from a standard roof truss?
o: A space frame is made of wood, while trusses are made of steel.
It is a 3D system that can span in two directions simultaneously, acting like a rigid plate.
A space frame is only used for interior ceilings, never for roofs.
It is a truss that only uses tension members.
questions.n: Space frames use a 3D network of triangles to distribute loads in all directions, allowing for massive column-free spans.

questions.q: When is a 'Post-and-Beam' system most appropriate over a Bearing Wall system?
o: When the building is located in a high-wind coastal area.
When the budget is extremely low and masonry is cheaper.
When the building needs to be more than 50 stories tall.
When large open spaces and flexible interior partition layouts are required.
questions.n: Because the walls aren't carrying the weight, they can be moved or replaced without collapsing the building.

questions.q: In a 'Bearing Wall System', what happens if you remove a wall to create a large door opening?
o: The building will remain stable because the floor slab will bridge the gap.
Nothing, because bearing walls only carry the weight of themselves.
The structural load path is interrupted, requiring a lintel or beam to redistribute the weight.
The wall will automatically become a non-bearing curtain wall.
questions.n: Removing a part of a bearing wall creates a 'hole' in the support system that must be reinforced to prevent collapse.

questions.q: What is the primary structural 'Tube' in a high-rise Tube System?
o: A giant steel pipe hidden inside the main stairwell.
The plumbing pipes that run from the basement to the roof.
The elevator shafts in the center of the building.
The perimeter frame of closely spaced columns and deep spandrel beams.
questions.n: In a Tube System, the exterior walls are designed to be so rigid that the entire building acts like a hollow straw/tube.

questions.q: What is the risk of using a 'Flat Slab' (no beams) in an area with high seismic activity?
o: The slab is too heavy and will crush the columns.
The slab will catch fire more easily.
Punching Shear failure at the column-slab connection during swaying.
The lack of beams makes the building too light to stay on the ground.
questions.n: Without beams or 'drop panels' to distribute the force, the column can 'punch' through the slab during an earthquake.

questions.q: Why would an architect choose a Steel Frame over Reinforced Concrete for a high-rise in a busy urban center?
o: Steel is much cheaper than concrete in the Philippines.
Lighter weight reduces foundation costs, and prefabrication speeds up on-site assembly.
Steel frame buildings do not require any inspections.
Steel is easier to mold into complex, curvy shapes on site.
questions.n: Steel's high strength-to-weight ratio allows for smaller foundations and faster 'dry' construction.

questions.q: In Post-tensioned concrete, why are the tendons 'pulled' after the concrete hardens?
o: To introduce internal compressive stress that counteracts future tension from loads.
To make the concrete dry faster.
Because the steel is too hot to pull when the concrete is wet.
To keep the steel from rusting.
questions.n: By 'pre-compressing' the concrete, you prevent it from cracking when it eventually tries to bend under a load.

questions.q: Which of these is the most effective way to prevent a 'Cold Joint'?
o: Ensuring a continuous pour and vibratory re-blending of the new and old layers.
Waiting at least 24 hours between pours to ensure the first one is hard.
Adding more water to the old concrete to make it wet again.
Painting the first layer with oil before the second layer arrives.
questions.n: The new pour must be placed and vibrated while the previous layer is still 'plastic' (not yet set).

questions.q: Why is the 'Lap Splice' length longer for tension bars than for compression bars?
o: Because steel is weaker in tension than in compression.
It isn't; compression laps are always longer in the Philippine Building Code.
Because tension tends to pull bars apart, requiring more surface area to transfer stress safely.
Because tension bars are usually thicker.
questions.n: Tension relies entirely on the 'grip' (bond) of the concrete; compression can be partly transferred by end-bearing.

questions.q: If you see a diagonal crack near the support of a concrete beam, which component likely failed?
o: The Stirrups (Shear Reinforcement).
The concrete's compressive strength.
The decorative plaster finish.
The main longitudinal rebars.
questions.n: Stirrups are designed to 'sew' together diagonal shear cracks; if they are missing or insufficient, diagonal cracks appear.

questions.q: What is the 'Rule of Thumb' for Cambering a long-span beam?
o: Always camber 50mm regardless of the span length.
Camber the beam upward by an amount equal to the expected dead load deflection.
Camber the beam downward so water doesn't pool in the middle.
Only camber if the beam is made of wood.
questions.n: The goal is for the beam to become perfectly flat once the permanent weight of the building is applied.
